name: Design a Web Application Firewall
intent: Inspect every web request at the edge, block injection, scanning and abuse before it reaches the application, and do it with a few milliseconds of delay and without blocking real customers.
codeTitle: an anomaly-scoring WAF with detection-only mode
finalIntro: One malicious request and one innocent request through the finished firewall.
prompt: Design a web application firewall for an online shop that receives 200,000 requests per second at its peak. It must stop SQL injection, cross-site scripting, path traversal (requests that use ../ to reach other files), scanners, credential-stuffing bots (bots that try stolen passwords) and floods of requests, without blocking real customers, and without adding noticeable delay. Security engineers need to change rules every day.
functional: Inspect each request's URL, headers, cookies and body before it reaches the application
Block, allow, or only log a request according to the rules
Score requests from several weak signals rather than relying on one rule
Limit requests per client, per path and per account, and detect automated clients
Let security engineers write exceptions, test new rules in detection-only mode, and publish rule changes
Record every decision so that a blocked customer can be explained
nonFunctional: Added latency under 5 ms at the 99th percentile
Rule changes reach every node in under a minute with no dropped connection
Real customers blocked by mistake well under 0.1% of requests
Keeps running at the peak and during a flood of attack traffic, by design degrading rather than falling over
A defined behaviour when the firewall itself is unhealthy: fail open (let traffic through) or fail closed (block it), chosen per route
Decisions are logged without slowing the request

firstAttempt.text: No firewall. Each application validates its own input, and a few developers add a check for quote characters and script tags in the code. Rate limiting is a counter inside each server.
limits: Every team writes its own checks, and some forget, so a single missed endpoint is an open door
A new attack technique needs a code change and a deployment in every application
Attack traffic reaches the application servers and consumes their capacity before anyone rejects it
Counters per server cannot see a client that spreads requests across all servers
There is no single place to see what was attacked and what was blocked

steps.title: Put an inline firewall in front of the application
steps.problem: Security checks scattered through application code are inconsistent, slow to change, and run only after the attack traffic has already reached the servers.
steps.fix: Run a reverse proxy at the edge that terminates TLS (it decrypts HTTPS), so it can see the request in plain text, and make it the only way in. Before looking at anything it normalises the request: it decodes percent-encoding (such as %3C for <) and other escapes, lowercases where case does not matter, collapses path tricks such as '/./' and '//', and enforces limits on header size, body size and method. It then inspects the URL, headers, cookies and body against rules, and only clean requests are forwarded to the application.
steps.tradeoff: One place enforces the same protection for every application and can change it without a deployment. It sees all traffic, so it adds latency to every request, becomes a critical dependency, and sees decrypted data that must be handled carefully. It also protects only what it understands: it does not replace validating input in the application.

steps.title: Score with rules, and start in detection-only mode
steps.problem: A rule that blocks on one match is either too loose to catch variants or so strict that it blocks real customers, for example a shopper searching for 'select a plan'.
steps.fix: Each rule adds points to an anomaly score for the request instead of deciding alone. A clear attack such as 'union select' adds 5, a weak sign such as the word 'select' adds 2, and a comment marker adds 2. The request is blocked only when the total reaches a threshold such as 5, so several weak signals together are blocked and one of them is not. Every new rule or threshold starts in detection-only mode: the verdict and the matched rules are logged but nothing is blocked, and the team reviews what would have been blocked, writes exceptions for the false positives, and only then switches to blocking.
steps.tradeoff: False positives drop and the threshold becomes one understandable dial between safety and convenience. Scoring is harder to explain than a single rule, detection-only mode leaves attacks unblocked while it runs, and the rule set needs steady tuning for each application.

steps.title: Add rate-based rules
steps.problem: Credential stuffing, scraping and floods are made of requests that each look perfectly normal. No payload rule can catch them.
steps.fix: Count requests per key in a shared counter store: per client address, per client address and path, and per account name on the login route. A key that exceeds its limit in a window adds points to the anomaly score, or is blocked outright for the heavy hitters, and the response includes a retry delay. Limits differ by route: a few login attempts per minute but hundreds of page views. Counters are updated locally on each node and merged with the shared store every second or so, so a client that spreads requests across nodes is still seen.
steps.tradeoff: Floods and brute force are stopped without a signature, and the limit is a clear dial. Many real users share one address behind a company network or mobile carrier, so limits per address alone block innocent people, and the counters add state that has to be fast and bounded.

steps.title: Detect bots with several signals
steps.problem: Attackers rotate addresses and copy a browser's headers, so address-based limits and simple user-agent checks no longer separate a person from a script.
steps.fix: Combine many weak signals into a bot score: a user agent that names a known tool, the order and set of headers compared with the browser that was claimed, the TLS fingerprint of the connection, a client address from a data centre, the speed and regularity of requests, and whether the client runs a JavaScript challenge and sends back a signed token. Low scores pass, middle scores get a challenge that a real browser solves invisibly, and high scores are blocked. Known good bots such as search engines are verified by reverse lookup and allowed.
steps.tradeoff: Automated abuse is cut without asking people to solve puzzles. It is an arms race, a challenge adds delay and breaks clients without JavaScript such as an API consumer or an accessibility tool, and the signals can be wrong for privacy tools and shared networks.

steps.title: Update rules without downtime
steps.problem: A new vulnerability is announced in the morning and the rule must protect every node within minutes, but a bad rule can block the whole site, and a restart drops connections.
steps.fix: Rules are data, not code. A publisher compiles them into a versioned, signed bundle, validates it against a library of known-good and known-bad requests, and puts it in the rule store. Nodes pull the new version, load it into memory next to the running one, and swap a single pointer, so requests in flight finish on the old version and new ones use the new one. The rollout is staged: detection-only first, then blocking on a small share of traffic, then everywhere, with automatic rollback if the block rate jumps or errors rise. The previous version stays loaded.
steps.tradeoff: Protection can arrive in minutes with no dropped connection, and a mistake is undone by swapping back. A staged rollout is slower than an emergency push, so urgent rules need a fast path with extra review, and every node briefly holds two rule sets in memory.

steps.title: Decide how it fails, and keep the delay small
steps.problem: The firewall sits on every request. If it is slow, overloaded or crashed, either all traffic is blocked or all traffic is unprotected, and both are bad.
steps.fix: Put a load balancer in front of a fleet of firewall nodes that autoscales on CPU, checks the health of each node, and drains a failing one. Set a time budget for inspection, for example 5 ms: if the engine cannot finish in time, the request takes a per-route default. Public content such as product pages fails open, so a firewall outage does not take the shop offline, while payment, login and admin routes fail closed. When the fleet is unreachable, the load balancer can route straight to the application only for routes marked fail-open. To keep latency down, inspect the headers and the first part of the body, cap the body size, compile rules to one pass over the text, and skip static files.
steps.tradeoff: An outage of the firewall no longer means an outage of the site, and delay stays predictable. Failing open for some routes accepts a window with weaker protection, an inspection limit lets an attacker hide a payload past the cap, and the extra hop and fleet cost money.

failures.scenario: A new rule blocks real customers
failures.impact: A rule published at noon matches a common product name, and checkouts start returning 403 for thousands of people.
failures.answer: The staged rollout watches the block rate and the share of blocked requests that belong to logged-in users with a good history. The jump trips the automatic rollback within a minute, swapping back to the previous rule version. The rule goes back to detection-only mode, an exception is written, and the false positive is added to the test library so it is caught before publishing next time.

failures.scenario: The firewall nodes crash or become overloaded during an attack
failures.impact: Traffic either stops, for fail closed, or reaches the application without inspection, for fail open.
failures.answer: The load balancer removes unhealthy nodes, the fleet autoscales, and cheap rules run first so a flood is dropped early (for instance by an address on a blocklist). If inspection takes longer than its budget, each route uses its own default: fail open for public pages, fail closed for login and payment. Alerts fire as soon as requests are being passed uninspected.

failures.scenario: An attacker encodes the payload to evade the rules
failures.impact: A double-encoded, mixed-case or split payload reaches the application because the rules only matched the plain form.
failures.answer: Normalisation runs before rules and repeats until the text stops changing, with a limit on the number of rounds. Requests that need more rounds than a normal client ever does are themselves suspicious and score points. The application still validates and parameterises its queries, because the firewall is a second layer and not a replacement.

failures.scenario: Many real users share one address
failures.impact: An office or mobile carrier with thousands of users sends many requests from one address, and a limit per address blocks all of them.
failures.answer: Limits are keyed on more than the address: a session cookie or token once present, the account on login routes, and the address together with the path. The bot score decides whether to challenge instead of block. Known corporate ranges can have higher limits, and a block is a challenge or a short delay before it is a ban.

failures.scenario: A zero-day exploit has no known signature
failures.impact: Attack requests do not match any existing rule, and the application is vulnerable until a patch exists.
failures.answer: A virtual patch is written as a narrow rule for the exact path and parameter, tested in detection-only mode for a few minutes against live traffic, and rolled out through the fast path. Anomaly scoring, rate rules and bot scoring may already slow the attack, and the application team ships the real fix.

alternatives.title: Where the firewall runs

options.name: A managed WAF at the CDN edge
options.pro: Absorbs floods far from the origin, no fleet to operate and global rules from the provider
options.con: Less control over rules, data leaves your network, and the origin must be locked to the CDN

options.name: A fleet of your own proxies
options.pro: Full control of rules, latency and data
options.con: You run and scale it, and a flood has to be absorbed by your own network

options.name: A module inside each application server
options.pro: No extra hop and it knows the application
options.con: Attack traffic still reaches the servers, and every team must keep it up to date

alternatives.pick: A managed edge WAF for the first line, with your own rules layered on it, and application validation underneath.

alternatives.title: How to decide that a request is bad

options.name: Block on the first matching rule
options.con: Every rule must be precise, which means evasions pass or customers are blocked

options.name: Anomaly scoring with a threshold
options.pro: Combines weak signals and gives one tunable dial
options.con: Harder to explain, and the threshold needs tuning

options.name: A learned model on request features
options.pro: Can catch variants no rule describes
options.con: Needs labelled data, is hard to explain to a blocked customer, and can be probed by attackers

alternatives.pick: Anomaly scoring, with a model as one more input to the score and not as the decider.

alternatives.title: What happens when the firewall is broken

options.name: Fail open
options.con: Attacks pass uninspected during the failure

options.name: Fail closed
options.con: The firewall's failure is a full outage

options.name: Choose per route
options.pro: Public pages stay up while login and payment stay protected
options.con: Needs a route list that is maintained and tested

alternatives.pick: Per route: open for public content, closed for login, payment and admin.

alternatives.title: How to roll out a new rule

options.name: Detection-only first, then a share of traffic, then all
options.pro: False positives are seen before they hurt anyone
options.con: Slower, and attacks pass during the trial

options.name: Test only in a staging environment
options.con: Staging traffic does not look like real traffic, so false positives are missed

alternatives.pick: Detection-only on live traffic first, with a fast path and a quick rollback for emergencies.

roles.label: Clients
roles.description: Customers, bots and attackers sending requests.

roles.label: Inspection points
roles.description: The load balancer and the firewall nodes that every request passes through.

roles.label: Event log
roles.description: Decisions on their way to storage and review, off the request path.

roles.label: Decision logic
roles.description: Rule engine, bot scoring, rule publisher and the application itself.

roles.label: Rules and counters
roles.description: Rule bundles, request counters and the application database.

quiz.question: A shop firewall blocks any request containing the word 'select' to stop SQL injection. A customer searching for 'select a plan' gets a 403. The security team still wants to catch real injection strings. What is the best change?
options: Remove the 'select' rule for the search route and rely on the application to validate the input of that route alone
Keep the rule but lower the inspected body size limit, so that short search phrases are skipped by the engine
Give each rule points in an anomaly score, so a weak sign adds 2 and a clear attack adds 5, and block at a total of 5
Apply the block only to requests that arrive over plain HTTP, since attackers rarely probe over HTTPS
quiz.explanation: Scoring lets several weak signals add up to a block while a single common word does not. A clear attack such as 'union select' still reaches the threshold alone. Removing the rule for a route leaves that endpoint open, and size limits or protocol checks have nothing to do with whether the text is an attack.

quiz.question: A login route allows 5 attempts per minute per client address. An office of 3,000 staff sits behind one public address and its users start getting blocked at the start of every workday. How should the limits change?
options: Count per account and per address with the path, and challenge a heavy address before it is banned outright
Raise the per-address limit to 5,000 per minute for every address so that offices are never blocked
Drop rate limits on the login route and rely on a bot score that blocks automated user agents and data centre addresses
Count attempts per application server instead of per address, so that the load is shared evenly across the fleet
quiz.explanation: A shared address hides many people, so the key should include the account and the path, and an excess should first get a challenge. A limit of 5,000 per address opens the route to credential stuffing from one address. User-agent checks are easy to fake, and counters per server cannot see a client spread across servers.

quiz.question: The firewall has a 5 ms inspection budget. During a flood, 30% of requests exceed it. The site has public product pages, a login route and a payment route. Which timeout default per route is best?
options: Fail open everywhere: an outage costs more than a brief window of weaker protection on any route
Fail closed on every route, so that no request ever reaches the application without being inspected first
Fail open on login and payment, because paying customers are the real users, and closed on product pages
Fail open on product pages, closed on login and payment, and alert when uninspected requests pass
quiz.explanation: Product pages can be served without inspection so a firewall problem does not take the shop offline, while login and payment are the targets worth protecting even at the cost of errors. Failing open everywhere exposes credentials and payments. Failing closed everywhere turns a slow firewall into a full outage. Failing open on login and payment but closed on product pages reverses the risk.
